---
title: "09 · Model selection"
subtitle: "Week 3"
---

::: {.guiding-q}
How do I select the best model?
:::

## In this session

- What "best" means: testing hypotheses vs. predicting well
- Full–null model comparisons and likelihood-ratio tests
- Information criteria (AIC) and multi-model inference
- Overfitting, and why stepwise selection is a problem
- Pre-specifying the model as the default for confirmatory analyses

::: {.key-terms}
**Key terms:** [AIC (Akaike information criterion)](../../glossary.qmd#aic), [Likelihood-ratio test](../../glossary.qmd#lrt), [Full–null model comparison](../../glossary.qmd#full-null), [Overfitting](../../glossary.qmd#overfitting), [Model selection](../../glossary.qmd#model-selection)
:::

## Learning goals

After this session you can

- compare nested models with a likelihood-ratio test,
- use and interpret AIC for a set of candidate models,
- explain why selecting predictors by *p*-values inflates false positives.

## Simulate first

Adding predictors that are pure noise always increases R². A good model selection strategy must guard against this.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.2
set.seed(9)
n <- 40
noise <- as.data.frame(matrix(rnorm(n * 20), n))
y <- rnorm(n)                                    # y is unrelated to all predictors

r2 <- sapply(1:20, function(k)
  summary(lm(y ~ ., data = noise[, 1:k, drop = FALSE]))$r.squared)

plot(1:20, r2, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#c0392b",
     xlab = "Number of noise predictors", ylab = expression(R^2))
```
